title: Observability: logs, metrics, traces, and what deserves an alert
story:
When a request crossed one machine, that machine's log was the story. Now a request crosses many services and no single host holds the account of what happened to it — the evidence is scattered across machines that do not know about each other, and the interesting failures are in the seams rather than inside any one component.

Three shapes of evidence answer three different questions, and the useful discipline is knowing which question you are asking. Metrics are aggregated numbers over time: how many, how fast, how often failing. They are cheap, they cover everything, and aggregation is exactly what destroys the individual case — a percentile cannot tell you which request was slow. Logs are individual records of events: what this process did at this moment. They preserve the specifics and they are per-service, so reconstructing one journey across seven of them by correlating timestamps is the thing everybody has tried and nobody enjoys. Traces are the causal tree of one request across every service it touched, which is the shape that matches the question you actually have during an incident.

The tracing paper is worth reading for its design goals rather than its architecture: low overhead, application-level transparency, and ubiquitous deployment on a very large scale system. Transparency is the one that makes it work — because a common set of building blocks is used across the organisation's software, instrumenting those blocks generates trace information without application involvement, carrying a trace context associated with a thread and tracking it across asynchronous callbacks and remote calls. Tracing that requires every team to cooperate is tracing that covers the services that cooperated.

Two design choices are named as central to its success rather than incidental, and the second is the one people resist. Restricting instrumentation. And sampling — the finding being that a sample of just one out of thousands of requests provides sufficient information for many common uses of the tracing data. That is a real constraint rather than a caveat: the specific request a customer is complaining about is almost certainly not in your trace data, and a system designed to always have it would cost more than the system it observes. One further detail worth stealing: collection is out of band, because an in-band scheme returning trace data within response headers can affect application network dynamics — the observation changing the thing observed.

Which leaves alerting, where the rule is short. Alert on symptoms a user would recognise, not on causes. A page for high processor usage wakes someone for a condition that may harm nobody; a page for checkout failure rate wakes them for something that is, by construction, worth waking up for.

problem.name: Evidence about a distributed request
problem.shape: A request crosses many services and no single machine holds the account of what happened to it.
tell: diagnosing an incident means correlating timestamps across several services by hand
a percentile is known to be bad and no individual slow request can be found
alerts fire for conditions no user would notice
instrumentation is per-team and coverage is patchy
problem.move: Pick the shape of evidence that matches the question: aggregates for how often, records for what happened here, traces for where a request spent its time. Get tracing by instrumenting shared building blocks rather than asking every team to cooperate. Accept sampling as a design constraint. Alert on symptoms a user would recognise rather than on causes.
problem.invariant: Only a trace carries the causal relationship between work in different services, because only it propagates a context through every call the request makes.
problem.breaks: Tracing at volume must be sampled, so the individual request you are asked about is probably absent from the data — and the more specific the complaint, the less likely your tracing has the answer. Full capture is not a budget problem to be solved later, it is a different and much more expensive system.

cost.time: propagation overhead on every call, kept viable by sampling and by instrumenting shared libraries rather than applications
cost.space: trace storage, which is why the sampling rate rather than the retention period is usually the binding decision
cost.beats: correlating logs by timestamp across services, which is manual, error-prone and cannot establish causality

worked.problem: What does a trace show you that logs and metrics cannot?
worked.reasoning:
The causal structure of one request across services — which service called which, in what order, and where the time actually went. Neither of the others can supply that, for different reasons.

Metrics fail because aggregation discards the individual. A metric tells you the ninety-ninth percentile latency of a service is bad. It cannot tell you which request was slow, what it was doing, or what it was waiting on, because that information was averaged away at collection time. That is not a gap to be closed with more metrics; it is what a metric is.

Logs fail because they are per-process and have no notion of the whole. Each service records what it did, honestly and in detail, and nothing in those records connects your slow request in one service to the call it made into another. You can attempt reconstruction by correlating timestamps across seven services, which is the manual, error-prone thing everyone has tried, and clock skew across machines makes the ordering you infer unreliable — which is the concurrency lesson arriving in operational form.

A trace is the tree. It carries a context through every call, so the record in the seventh service is linked to the request that caused it, and you can see that the request spent most of its time in one dependency rather than guessing. That is the question you actually have during an incident.

The design constraints worth knowing come from the paper. It states the goals as low overhead, application-level transparency, and ubiquitous deployment at very large scale — and transparency is what makes it real. Because a common set of building blocks is used across the software, instrumenting those blocks generates trace information without application involvement, propagating context across asynchronous callbacks and remote calls. Tracing that requires every team to opt in covers the services that opted in, which is never the ones you need.

And the limitation I would raise unprompted, because people are surprised by it in incidents: it is sampled. The finding is that one request in thousands provides sufficient information for many common uses. So when someone asks why this specific request was slow, the honest answer is often that it was not sampled — and a system that always kept everything would be more expensive than the system it observes.

One implementation detail is worth stealing generally: collection is out of band, because returning trace data in response headers can affect application network dynamics. The instrument should not perturb the thing it measures.

problem.practice: Take your last incident and ask which of the three shapes actually told you what was wrong. Then check what fraction of requests your tracing samples, and work out whether a specific customer complaint from last week would be in the data. Finally, list your paging alerts and mark each as a symptom or a cause.

beats.broke: A request crosses many services, so no single machine holds the story of what happened to it, and the logs that would explain a failure are scattered across hosts that do not know about each other.
beats.fix: Emit three shapes of evidence — aggregated numbers over time, individual records of events, and a causal tree following one request across every service it touched — and make the third possible by carrying a context through every call.
beats.cost: Full capture is unaffordable at volume, so tracing is sampled, which means the specific request you are asked about is probably not in the data.

interview.q: What does a trace show you that logs and metrics cannot?
interview.trap: Describing it as richer logging. The distinguishing property is causal linkage across process boundaries — metrics aggregated the individual away and logs never had the relationship — and the honest limitation is that tracing is sampled, so the specific request being asked about is usually absent.
interview.answer:

Metrics fail because aggregation discards the individual. A metric tells you a service's high percentile is bad; it cannot tell you which request was slow or what it was waiting on, because that was averaged away at collection. That is not a gap to close with more metrics — it is what a metric is.

A trace is the tree: it carries a context through every call, so a record in the seventh service is linked to the request that caused it, and you can see where the time actually went rather than guessing.

The stated goals are low overhead, application-level transparency, and ubiquitous deployment at very large scale — and transparency is what makes it real, since instrumenting the shared building blocks generates traces without application involvement, propagating context across asynchronous callbacks and remote calls. The limitation I would raise unprompted is sampling: the finding is that one request in thousands suffices for many common uses, so when someone asks why a specific request was slow, the honest answer is often that it was not sampled — and always keeping everything would cost more than the system being observed.
